key_terms.meaning: The privileged core program that alone configures and reads hardware; everything else reaches hardware only through it.
The controlled entry point a user program uses to ask the kernel for a service, e.g. write() or a driver ioctl().
The protected memory region and CPU mode in which the kernel runs; a fault here can halt the whole system.
The restricted memory region and CPU mode where application tasks run; a fault here kills only that task.
Any unit of work the scheduler can run; in an RTOS it is usually a single thread with its own stack and priority.
A running program that owns a private address space, file table and at least one thread.
A flow of execution inside a process; shares the process address space and owns only its stack, registers and priority.
The saved state of a task: program counter, stack pointer, CPU registers and status flags.
Saving the context of the running task and restoring that of the next; it does no useful application work.
Time from the event that makes a higher-priority task ready to the first instruction of that task executing.
A task keeps the CPU until it volunteers to yield; one runaway loop starves all others.
The scheduler can stop a running task on a timer tick or a higher-priority wake-up; needed for bounded response time.
All cores are identical and run one OS image that schedules tasks across them.
Each core runs its own separate OS or bare-metal program; cores communicate through shared memory or a mailbox.
Fixed-priority rule: shorter period gets higher priority; schedulable if total utilisation U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1).
Dynamic-priority rule: the ready task with the nearest absolute deadline runs next; optimal, and needs U ≤ 1.
A counter with wait and signal operations used to signal an event or guard a counted resource; a binary semaphore is often used from an ISR to wake a task.
A lock with ownership: only the task that took it may release it, which allows priority inheritance.
A bounded FIFO buffer through which tasks or ISRs pass data items without sharing memory directly.
The board-specific set of boot code, clock, pin, memory and driver code that lets one OS image run on one board.
The small program that initialises the board, loads a kernel image and jumps to it.

takeaways: The kernel is the only code that touches hardware, and every other program reaches hardware through a system call.
A process owns an address space; threads of that process share it and cost only a stack plus a register context each.
Context switching is pure overhead, so an RTOS keeps it short and predictable rather than merely fast on average.
Rate monotonic scheduling is the fixed-priority rule for periodic tasks, and its utilisation bound tells you whether the set is safe.
EDF can schedule any set with utilisation at or below 1, but a transient overload makes it misbehave far worse than RM.
A hard real-time system fails when a deadline slips; an RTOS is engineered to bound the worst case, not the average.
A semaphore signals, a mutex protects, and a queue carries data; each solves a different inter-task problem.
A device driver hides register bit-fields behind a standard interface, and the BSP makes one OS boot on one board.
Embedded memory allocation must be bounded and deterministic, which usually means fixed-block pools instead of a general heap.
FreeRTOS and embedded Linux are the two ends of one choice: bounded worst case and size, versus features and throughput.
bank_note: Long answers for this unit are expected to combine definition and comparison with a worked schedulability or timing calculation, so carry numbers, a small task table and a clear architecture sketch into every answer.

bank.q: Define kernel, kernel space and user space. Trace what happens, step by step, when a user task calls write() to send a byte to a UART.
outline: Kernel is the privileged core that alone configures hardware; kernel space is its protected region and CPU mode; user space is the restricted region where tasks run
User task executes a trap or SVC instruction that switches to privileged mode and enters the kernel at a fixed vector
Kernel validates the arguments and the pointer range, then calls the registered UART driver routine
Driver writes the data register and polls or waits on the transmit-empty interrupt
Kernel returns to user mode with a result code; the task never loads a peripheral register itself

bank.q: Distinguish a task, a process and a thread. Why does a multitasking RTOS usually run one thread per task?
outline: Task: unit of scheduling; process: unit of resource ownership with its own address space; thread: unit of execution inside a process
Threads of one process share code, data and heap, and own only a stack, register context and priority
Creating a thread is cheaper than creating a process because no address space is copied
An RTOS task is a single thread plus stack and TCB, so the switch cost is one stack pointer and one register save
Sharing data between threads needs a mutex; between processes it needs shared memory or a queue

bank.q: Compare cooperative and preemptive multitasking, and AMP with SMP. Give one embedded example of each arrangement.
outline: Cooperative: task runs until it yields, so response time depends on other tasks' code and is unbounded
Preemptive: timer tick or higher-priority wake-up forces the switch; required for hard deadlines
AMP: each core has its own OS or bare-metal loop, e.g. one core runs a motor control loop, the other runs Linux
SMP: one OS schedules all tasks across identical cores; needs spinlocks in the kernel
State the cost: preemption needs reentrant code and critical sections; SMP needs cache coherency

bank.q: Explain rate monotonic scheduling. State its utilisation bound and compute the bound for n = 3.
outline: Periodic task model: each task has period T, worst-case execution time C, deadline equal to period
Rule: shorter period gets higher fixed priority; tasks are preemptive and independent
Utilisation U = Σ(Cᵢ/Tᵢ) with i from 1 to n
Bound U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1); for n = 3 it is about 0.780
If U is below the bound the set is guaranteed schedulable; above it, schedulability must be tested by timeline analysis
Worked example: C = 1,1,2 ms with T = 4,5,10 ms gives U = 0.25 + 0.20 + 0.20 = 0.65, hence safe

bank.q: Distinguish hard and soft real-time systems, and list the design differences between an RTOS and a general-purpose OS.
outline: Hard: a missed deadline is a system failure, e.g. airbag firing; soft: a missed deadline degrades quality, e.g. video frame drop
GPOS optimises average throughput and fairness; RTOS optimises worst-case latency
RTOS features: preemptive priority scheduler, priority inheritance, bounded interrupt latency, no demand paging, small deterministic kernel
GPOS features: virtual memory, large driver base, time-slicing of equal priorities, high but variable latency
Define jitter and show why a bounded maximum matters more than a small mean

bank.q: A task set has C = 1 ms, T = 5 ms; C = 2 ms, T = 10 ms; C = 3 ms, T = 20 ms. Test it under RM and under EDF, and state which rule you would ship.
outline: Tabulate the three tasks with period, execution time and priority order under RM
RM bound for n = 3 is about 0.780, and 0.55 is below it, so RM guarantees all deadlines
Draw the timeline for one hyperperiod of 20 ms and show response times
EDF is also feasible because U ≤ 1, but compare behaviour under a transient overload
Recommendation: RM for a fixed small set on a small kernel; EDF when utilisation is high or periods change

bank.q: Explain priority inversion with a three-task timeline, and show how a mutex with priority inheritance bounds it.
outline: Low-priority task L holds a mutex; high-priority task H blocks on it; medium task M preempts L and H waits for M
Show the unbounded wait on a timeline
Solution 1: priority inheritance, so L runs at H's priority while holding the lock
Solution 2: priority ceiling, so the lock is taken at the ceiling priority
Note the difference between a mutex (with inheritance) and a binary semaphore (without ownership)
Cost: inheritance adds code to the scheduler and complicates the ready queue

bank.q: Describe a context switch on a Cortex-M class microcontroller in an RTOS, and explain how switch latency is measured.
outline: Trigger: SysTick or an ISR makes a higher-priority task ready; kernel sets the pend bit
Hardware stacks the caller-saved registers automatically on exception entry
Kernel saves the remaining registers and the stack pointer into the current TCB
Scheduler picks the highest-priority ready task and loads its stack pointer from its TCB
Return from exception restores the new task's registers; cycle count of these steps gives switch latency
Measure by toggling a GPIO pin at entry and exit of the switch and reading the pulse on a scope

bank.q: Write the structure of two FreeRTOS tasks that pass a sensor reading through a queue and signal completion with a semaphore from an ISR.
outline: Declare a queue handle and a binary semaphore handle before the scheduler starts
Producer task reads the sensor and calls the queue send with a finite block time
Consumer task blocks on the queue receive and processes the value
ISR uses the FromISR variants and requests a yield if a higher-priority task was woken
Use a mutex, not a binary semaphore, for shared data with priority inheritance
Mention stack sizing per task and that ISRs must stay short; defer work to a task

bank.q: Design memory management for a board with 64 KB RAM and no MMU. Compare a fixed-block pool with malloc and show how fragmentation arises.
outline: No MMU means no protection between tasks; every pointer is physical
malloc gives variable-size blocks and suffers external fragmentation over long runtimes
Fixed-block pool: carve RAM into blocks of a few sizes at start-up; allocation is a list pop, so time is constant
Use static allocation for task stacks, queues and buffers wherever the count is known
Show a worst-case figure: a 512-byte block pool with 20 blocks gives a hard ceiling on memory use
Determinism: allocation and free must complete in bounded time for real-time use

bank.q: Describe the boot sequence of an embedded Linux board from power-on to a running shell, and place the bootloader, kernel image, initramfs and root file system in it.
outline: On-chip ROM code reads the boot mode pins and loads a first-stage loader from flash or SD card
First-stage loader sets clocks and DRAM, then loads U-Boot
U-Boot loads the kernel image and device tree into DRAM, passes the command line, and jumps
Kernel decompresses, initialises memory and drivers, then mounts initramfs as a temporary root
init runs, the real root file system is mounted from eMMC or flash, and services start
Mention JFFS2 for raw NOR flash, UBIFS for NAND with UBI, and that both survive power loss
Note recovery: a serial console and a bootloader prompt are the field-service path

bank.q: A team must choose between FreeRTOS on a microcontroller and embedded Linux on an applications processor for a UPI payment terminal. Justify a recommendation.
outline: List requirements: secure key handling, display and network stack, deadline for the card reader, cost per unit, power, field updates
FreeRTOS: few KB of RAM, microsecond-class bounded latency, small BSP, but no memory protection and a thin TCP/IP and file stack
Linux: full networking, TLS, file systems, driver base, but seconds-long boot unless tuned, and worst-case latency needs PREEMPT_RT
Cost check in rupees per board and the RAM and flash each option forces
Risk check: certified security module, update mechanism, and a bootloader that can recover from a failed update
Give a clear verdict with the condition that would reverse it

bank.q: A prototype uses malloc inside an interrupt handler, a binary semaphore in place of a mutex, and a long polling loop inside an ISR. Assess the risks and propose a corrected design.
outline: malloc in an ISR: unbounded time and possible lock contention, so latency is not bounded; memory should be preallocated
Binary semaphore for shared data: no ownership and no priority inheritance, so priority inversion is unbounded; use a mutex
Long ISR: blocks all lower and equal priority interrupts, adds jitter to every task; split into top half and deferred task
Corrected design: ISR captures the value, signals a task, returns; the task does the work
Add measurement: GPIO pulse widths to record ISR and switch latency
State the verification step: timeline analysis or a worst-case execution time measurement before release

bank.q: Explain the layers of a board support package and how a device driver written for one board becomes a standard interface for application code.
outline: BSP layers: boot code and clock and pin setup, memory map, interrupt controller setup, peripheral drivers, and the OS adaptation layer
Driver exposes open, read, write, ioctl on a device node or a handle, hiding register bit-fields
Example: an application sends characters to a UART without knowing the baud divisor register
Porting cost: to move to a new board you change the BSP, not the application
Kernel versus user space: a kernel driver runs privileged and can be reached from a task by a system call
Mention device tree as the data-driven alternative on embedded Linux

glossary.def: The privileged core of an operating system that manages CPU, memory and devices and is entered only through controlled entry points.
A software trap by which a user task requests a kernel service such as a file write or a device operation.
The unprivileged execution mode and memory region where application tasks run, isolated from hardware registers.
A schedulable unit of work, usually a single thread with its own stack, priority and control block in an RTOS.
A program in execution that owns a private address space, open files and one or more threads.
An execution path within a process that shares the process address space but has its own stack and register state.
The complete saved state of a task, comprising program counter, stack pointer, CPU registers and status flags.
The act of saving one task's context and restoring another's, which consumes CPU time without doing application work.
Forcibly removing a running task from the CPU when a higher-priority task becomes ready or a time slice expires.
A scheduling rule that gives each ready task of equal priority a fixed time slice in turn.
A fixed-priority rule assigning higher priority to tasks with shorter periods.
A dynamic-priority rule that always runs the ready task whose absolute deadline is nearest.
The fraction of CPU time demanded, U = Σ(Cᵢ/Tᵢ) for execution time C and period T.
A class of system in which missing a deadline is a functional failure and may be unsafe.
A class of system in which a missed deadline only reduces quality of service.
The variation in the time a task takes to respond or in the period between successive runs.
A counter with wait and signal operations used to signal an event or guard a counted resource.
A lock that only its owner may release, allowing the kernel to apply priority inheritance.
A situation where a high-priority task waits behind a low-priority task that is itself delayed by a middle-priority task.
A protocol in which a task holding a lock runs at the priority of the highest task waiting for it.
A bounded first-in-first-out buffer used to pass data between tasks or from an interrupt to a task.
Code that translates a peripheral's registers and interrupts into a standard interface for the rest of the system.
The board-specific collection of boot code, clock, pin, memory and driver code that lets an OS run on that board.
A small program that initialises the board, loads a kernel image into memory and transfers control to it.
The loss of usable memory when free space is split into pieces too small to satisfy a request.
The property that an operation completes within a known worst-case bound, not merely quickly on average.
